title: Buy Now, Maybe Pay Later: Dealing with Prompt-Tax While Staying at the Frontier - Andrew Thomspson

primary.label: Prompting & LLM Programming

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's central concept is 'prompt tax' and it focuses extensively on prompt design, prompt library management, and prompt migration strategies across model upgrades in a production agentic system. Orbital serves real-estate legal due diligence workflows, while the prompt management lessons are broadly applicable across domains. The talk covers production deployment, ongoing maintenance of prompt-heavy AI systems, and model migration challenges across frontier model upgrades. Requires familiarity with agentic systems, prompt engineering, and model migration concepts to fully appreciate the strategies discussed. Conference presentation delivered at the AI Engineer channel. All evidence is drawn from a practitioner's 18 months of production experience shared verbally, with no peer-reviewed or experimental validation.

summary: Andrew Thompson, CTO of Orbital (~80 people, half in product engineering, offices in New York and London), introduces "prompt tax" as the hidden cost incurred when frontier LLMs upgrade and existing prompts break. The talk covers four sections: the pain of progress, shipping at the frontier, battle-tested tactics, and questions about paying back prompt tax. Orbital automates real-estate due diligence via its Co-pilot product, which OCRs documents, creates agentic plans broken into subtasks each running its own agentic system with multiple LLM calls, extracts information with clickable citations, and produces downloadable reports. Over 18 months, Orbital grew from under 1 billion to nearly 20 billion tokens per month and from zero to multiple seven figures in ARR. Their model journey spanned GPT-3.5 through GPT-4 32K, 4 Turbo, 4.1, and system 2 models from o1 preview to o4 mini. Three strategic decisions stand out: optimizing prompting over fine-tuning for speed, heavy reliance on domain-expert lawyers who write 1,000+ domain-specific prompts, and choosing "vibes over evals." Prompt tax is explicitly distinguished from technical debt. Migration tactics include stripping how-instructions for system 2 models (which prefer clear objectives and time to reason, not constraints), leveraging thought tokens for user explainability and debugging, applying feature-flag-style progressive rollouts, and using new models to self-migrate old prompts. Thompson addresses change aversion bias—the heightened anxiety of moving to unknown systems—and introduces the "betting on the model" mantra: build for where models will be in 3-6-12 months, not just today. He emphasizes the need for brave shipping calls and rapid feedback loops where domain experts fix prompts in minutes or hours. A Demis Hassabis quote underscores the uniquely fast-evolving AI tech stack and the value of deeply technical product AI engineers. The final section asks whether eval systems can scale as product surface area grows, acknowledges that comprehensive evals may be prohibitively expensive and slow, and proposes progressive delivery calibrated on feedback volume as the primary tactic. The central thesis: buy now to stay at the frontier; whether you pay later is case-by-case. Thompson closes by hinting that once Orbital builds and rolls out an eval system, he may deliver a future presentation on its trials and tribulations and whether it resolves the issues raised.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: "Prompt tax" is the hidden cost of upgrading frontier LLMs—prompts break, regressions appear, and unknown unknowns create fear—distinct from technical debt.
Orbital scaled from <1B to ~20B tokens/month and from zero to multiple seven figures ARR in 18 months using an agentic system for real-estate due diligence.
System 2 models prefer clear objectives with room to reason; strip how-instructions and unnecessary constraints from system 1 prompts during migration.
"Betting on the model" mantra: build features anticipating models will get smarter, cheaper, and faster in 3-6-12 months rather than optimizing for today's limitations.
Use new models to self-migrate domain-specific prompts, radically reducing manual human effort.
Rapid feedback loops—user feedback routed to domain experts who fix and ship prompts—can resolve issues in minutes or hours versus traditional days or weeks.
Comprehensive eval systems may be prohibitively expensive and slow for complex agentic products; progressive delivery calibrated on feedback volume is a pragmatic alternative.
Central thesis: ship now ("buy now") to stay at the AI frontier; whether you pay the prompt tax later is determined case-by-case.

sections.title: Introduction to Prompt Tax
sections.summary: Thompson introduces the concept of prompt tax using a birthday bike analogy: new AI models bring exciting functionality but also unintended consequences from probabilistic systems. The talk covers four sections: pain of progress, shipping at frontier, battle-tested tactics, and questions about paying back prompt tax.

sections.title: Orbital: Real Estate Due Diligence Agentic Product
sections.summary: Thompson describes Orbital's mission to automate real estate due diligence, team structure (~80 people, half engineering, with embedded domain experts), and demonstrates the Orbital Co-pilot product that OCRs documents, breaks tasks into agentic subtasks with multiple LLM calls, and generates reports with clickable citations.

sections.title: Growth Metrics and Model Journey
sections.summary: Over 18 months, Orbital scaled from <1B to ~20B tokens/month and from zero to multiple seven figures ARR. The model journey spans GPT-3.5, GPT-4 32K, GPT-4 Turbo, GPT-4.1, and system 2 models from o1 preview to o4 mini.

sections.title: Three Key Strategic Decisions
sections.summary: Thompson articulates three decisions: (1) optimize prompting over fine-tuning for development speed, (2) heavy reliance on domain-expert lawyers who write 1,000+ domain-specific prompts, (3) choosing vibes over evals—subjective human testing rather than rigorous evaluation systems.

sections.title: Prompt Tax Mechanics and Migration Approach
sections.summary: Explains that more prompts equal more prompt tax. When new models drop, the team experiments, assesses migration cost, and manages fear of unknowns. Prompt tax is distinguished from technical debt. The migration strategy involves releasing to subsets of users, fixing issues quickly, then rolling out broadly.

sections.title: Battle-Tested Tactics: System 1 vs System 2 and Thought Tokens
sections.summary: System 1 models required specifying how and repeating instructions; system 2 models need only clear objectives with room to reason, so constraints and redundant instructions should be stripped. Thought tokens from system 2 models can be surfaced to users for explainability (valuable for lawyers) and used internally for debugging.

sections.title: Change Aversion Bias and Betting on the Model
sections.summary: Feature-flag-style progressive rollouts mitigate risk, but change aversion bias heightens anxiety around new models—simply announcing a change makes everyone hyperaware of issues. The 'betting on the model' mantra encourages building for where models will be in 3-6-12 months. Using system 2 models to self-migrate domain-specific prompts radically reduces manual effort.

sections.title: Tough Calls and Rapid Feedback Loops
sections.summary: Shipping new models requires a person or team brave enough to take on risk and deal with consequences after shipping. A strong feedback loop—user feedback routed through the product to domain experts who evaluate, fix prompts, and ship to production—can resolve issues in minutes or hours versus traditional days or weeks.

sections.title: Demis Hassabis and the AI Engineering Opportunity
sections.summary: A Demis Hassabis quote from the Hard Fork podcast highlights that the AI tech stack itself is evolving faster than prior revolutionary technologies, requiring deeply technical product people who can intercept where technology will be in a year. Thompson sees product AI engineers—connecting model capabilities to user needs—as the future of the AI engineering community.

sections.title: Paying the Prompt Tax: Evals, Progressive Delivery, and Central Thesis
sections.summary: Thompson questions whether vibes-based testing will scale as product surface area grows and whether eval systems are the answer—acknowledging that comprehensive evals covering correctness, style, conciseness, and citation accuracy may be prohibitively expensive, slow, or impossible. Progressive delivery calibrated on feedback volume is proposed as the primary tactic. The central thesis: buy now to stay at the frontier; whether you pay later is case-by-case. He closes by hinting that once Orbital builds and rolls out an eval system, he may deliver a future presentation on its trials and tribulations and whether it resolves the issues raised here.
